prompt: Which of these is a strategic decision for Varanda?

choices.text: Moving six stops from a late truck to one that is ahead
choices.why: Minutes, one person on the floor, easy to undo: operational, lesson 14.

choices.text: Shifting R$ 15 thousand of December's media from social ads to search
choices.why: A month, a manager, a budget line: tactical, lesson 15.

choices.text: Opening the first store outside Minas Gerais
choices.why: Right: a ten-year lease and a team, decided by the board.

choices.text: Choosing which garden products to reorder this week for the warehouse
choices.why: Frequent and reversible; lesson 9 even handed it to a rule.

prompt: Why does the board get fewer numbers than Renata's monthly review, over a longer period?
hint: What are the board's questions about?

choices.text: Board members have less time than managers, so each page has to be short
choices.why: Time is not the lesson's argument; the kind of question is.

choices.text: Its questions are about direction, which shows only in a long series
choices.why: Right: few numbers over years, because a month says nothing about where the company is heading.

choices.text: Detailed numbers are confidential and may not leave the departments
choices.why: The board can see anything; it is shown less because more would not help it decide.

choices.text: Annual numbers are audited, and monthly ones are not reliable enough for anybody
choices.why: Renata decides on closed monthly numbers every month; reliability is not the difference.

prompt: Which properties does a number in a strategic pack have, by the lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: It is annual, closed and checked
choices.why: Right: the board decides on the year as finance closed it.

choices.text: It refreshes every ten minutes
choices.why: That is the operational board of lesson 14.

choices.text: It is compared over years and against the plan
choices.why: Right: the plan is what the company meant to become.

choices.text: It sits beside data from outside the company
choices.why: Right: prices, the market, competitors.

choices.text: It is broken down by store and by channel
choices.why: That detail belongs to the later pages and the monthly reviews.

prompt: A retailer's sales grew 6% in a year when prices rose 4% and its market grew 8%. What is the strategic reading?
hint: Two outside comparisons, two different losses.

choices.text: A healthy year: 6% is above inflation
choices.why: Above inflation, yes, by about 1.9%, and still well behind its market.

choices.text: It grew about 1.9% in real terms and lost share of its market
choices.why: Right: 1.06 ÷ 1.04 is about 1.9% real, and growing slower than the market means a smaller share of it.

choices.text: It shrank, because 6% minus 4% minus 8% is negative
choices.why: Its sales did not shrink in real terms; prices and the market are two separate comparisons, not one sum.

choices.text: Nothing can be said without the competitors' figures, which a private company does not publish
choices.why: The market figure already answers the share question.

prompt: Every row of Varanda's board page is a little below plan. Why is the page built to be read as a whole?
hint: What happens to each row alone?

choices.text: Because the law requires a board to see the indicators together
choices.why: No law is involved; the reason is what the rows say together.

choices.text: Because the plan is the sum of the five rows
choices.why: The plan has a value per row; they are not added.

choices.text: Because the rows share a scale, so they can be compared directly on the sparklines
choices.why: Each sparkline is scaled to its own row; the reading is about meaning, not scale.

choices.text: Alone, each is explained away; together they show real growth, productivity and online all stalling
choices.why: Right: none of the five says it, and the five together do.

prompt: The plan was revised last year, closer to what Varanda achieved. Why does the page still compare 2025 with the plan approved in 2022?
hint: A target that moves towards the result.

choices.text: A target revised towards the result tells the board less each time
choices.why: Right: judging against a moving target is how a pack stops telling the board anything.

choices.text: The revised plan has not been audited, so it cannot be shown to the board
choices.why: Plans are not audited; the reason is about what the comparison can tell.

choices.text: The 2022 plan is in nominal reais and the revised one is in real terms, so only the first fits the page
choices.why: The lesson says nothing of the kind; the point is that the target moved.

choices.text: Comparing with an older plan makes the results look better
choices.why: Here it does the opposite: the older plan is the more demanding one.

prompt: The first page of the board pack shows five numbers over five years, each beside the ___ the board approved.
hint: The strategic version of Renata's budget.

prompt: In 2025 Varanda's nine stores sold R$ 82.39 million on 20,500 square metres of floor. What did each square metre sell, in reais, rounded to a whole real?
hint: Millions times 1,000,000, divided by square metres.

prompt: A company's sales went from 100 in 2021 to 150 in 2025. What is the compound annual growth rate, in per cent, to one decimal?
A year's sales were 110 in reais of that year, and its price index was 110 (base year = 100). What were they in base-year reais?
hint: Divide by the index, multiply by 100.

prompt: Why does the CAGR from 2021 to 2025 use ^(1/4) and not ^(1/5)?

choices.text: The first year is a base year and is left out of the table
choices.why: 2021 is in the table; it is the starting point of the four steps.

choices.text: A quarter of a year is lost to the close of the books
choices.why: The close has nothing to do with the exponent.

choices.text: Five years of figures hold four years of growth
choices.why: Right: from the first figure to the last there are four steps; with 5 the formula answers 6.2.

choices.text: The fourth root removes inflation, which a fifth root would leave in the result
choices.why: Inflation is removed by the index column, not by the exponent.

prompt: A store's sales grew 8% in a year when prices rose 5%. What was its real growth?
hint: Divide the growth factors; do not subtract the rates.

choices.text: About 13%, since both raise what the store takes
choices.why: Adding the rates counts the price rise as growth twice over.

choices.text: Exactly 3%, the difference between the two
choices.why: Subtracting is a close shortcut, not exact: 1.08 ÷ 1.05 is a little under 3%.

choices.text: About 2.9%, from 1.08 divided by 1.05
choices.why: Right: the real factor is the nominal factor divided by the price factor.

choices.text: Still 8%, because a price index does not change how many units were sold in the store that year
choices.why: Real growth is about what the reais buy; ignoring prices is the nominal figure again.

prompt: Put in order the steps to a real compound annual growth rate for 2021 to 2025.
items: Type each year's sales beside its price index
Divide each year's sales by its index and multiply by 100
Divide the last real figure by the first
Raise the ratio to 1/4 and subtract 1
trap: Computing the nominal rate first and subtracting inflation at the end is the tempting shortcut, and it is only approximately right.

prompt: Why does taking Ipatinga's R$ 7.04 million out of 2025 lower Varanda's nominal CAGR from 7.9% to 5.9%, and why does it matter?

choices.text: Ipatinga's sales were counted twice in 2025 and the correction removes the duplicate
choices.why: Nothing was counted twice; the sales are real and they come from a store that did not exist in 2021.

choices.text: Part of the growth was bought by opening a store, not earned by the existing ones
choices.why: Right: total growth mixes the two, and lesson 18's like-for-like separates them.

choices.text: A new store loses money in its first years, which hides the growth
choices.why: The lesson says nothing about Ipatinga's profit; the point is where the growth came from.

choices.text: Its sales are in a different currency
choices.why: Everything is in reais; the store simply was not there in 2021.

prompt: Match each perspective of the balanced scorecard with the Varanda measure the lesson puts in it.
hint: From the owners down to the people.

pairs.right: Sales per square metre in real terms
Share of customers who buy again within a year

prompt: What does the lesson say is missing from a board pack that is all money?

choices.text: The monthly detail behind each annual figure
choices.why: Monthly detail is in the later pages; adding it would not show causes.

choices.text: The causes of the results it shows
choices.why: Right: money is the lagging result; the other perspectives show what drives it.

choices.text: The competitors' financial results, which a strategic page has to set beside its own
choices.why: Outside data matters, but it is more money; the gap the lesson names is causes.

choices.text: A single north star metric to replace the five rows
choices.why: The lesson says a north star does not replace a board page.

prompt: Varanda's online team adopts a north star: orders delivered complete and on the promised date each month. What is the risk the lesson names?

choices.text: It is a lagging indicator, so it cannot guide a team
choices.why: It moves monthly with what the team does; the risk is how it gets raised.

choices.text: Counting it needs data the warehouse does not record
choices.why: Deliveries and promised dates are recorded; lesson 10 measured them.

choices.text: Raised alone, it climbs if the promised date is simply moved further out
choices.why: Right: one number everybody pushes gets raised in ways that do not help, so it needs a counter-metric.

choices.text: A north star is meant for technology companies and does not fit a retailer that has stores
choices.why: The lesson gives a retail example; the limit is gaming, not the industry.

prompt: Read from the bottom up, each lower row of the scorecard is a ___ indicator of the row above it.
Caio asks for his twelve weekly warehouse indicators to go on the board page, "so the board sees operations". What fits this lesson?
hint: One measure per perspective, chosen by a board question.

choices.text: Add the twelve, since a balanced scorecard needs operational measures
choices.why: Twelve rows is the twenty-number page lesson 11 warned about.

choices.text: Add the one a board decision depends on, such as stock-outs for the warehouse question
choices.why: Right: one per perspective, each tied to a question on the board's table.

choices.text: Add none, since operations belong in Caio's review
choices.why: The internal-process perspective belongs on the page; the question is how many and which.

choices.text: Average the twelve into one operations score
choices.why: An average of twelve unlike things says nothing anybody can act on.

prompt: A competitor announces that its sales grew 30% over three years, a period in which prices rose 15% in total. What did it grow in real terms over the three years?

choices.text: About 13.0%
Exactly 15%, the difference between 30% and 15%
choices.why: Subtracting overstates it here: the factors divide, they do not subtract.

choices.text: About 10% a year, which is 30% shared over the three years
choices.why: That is a nominal yearly figure, and wrongly divided; the question asks for real growth over the period.

choices.text: 30%, since a competitor's own figures are already adjusted for prices
choices.why: Sales announced in reais are nominal unless the announcement says otherwise.

prompt: Lessons 14 to 16: match each level with the screen that serves it at Varanda.

pairs.right: Exceptions for the next hour, the time of the data in the header
The month against budget and last year, with an action list
Five years against the plan, with prices and the market beside them

right_distractors: Every department's dashboard on one page
